title: Build a cup from volumes
objective: Organize a cup as a cylindrical body and a looped handle, then revise the construction to match what you observe.

warmup.instructions: Keep a handled cup in one place. Spend four minutes making one loose cylinder guide beside it, with a center axis and top and base ellipses. For the last three minutes, compare the guide's width, rim opening, and side angle with your actual cup; note one correction.

explanation: A cylinder can be organized with a center axis, top and base ellipses, and side edges. This is a light starting guide: a real cup may taper or lean, so check each side against the silhouette you see.
Build the handle as a separate loop. Compare its opening and two attachment points with the cup, then revise the construction before strengthening a few visible edges.

exercise.instructions:
1. (4 min) Place a handled cup where you can keep the same view. Choose an angle that shows the opening and handle; compare its overall height and width.
2. (5 min) Lightly mark a center axis and the cup's outer height. Leave the construction easy to change.
3. (7 min) Draw the rim as you observe it. Extend the sides into a cylinder-like body, follow any taper, and lightly place the base.
4. (8 min) Add the handle as a separate loop. Compare its opening and mark both places where it joins the cup.
5. (5 min) Look back and compare the rim tilt, body taper, and handle spacing. Correct one mismatch against the object.
6. (2 min) Strengthen only the visible edges; keep useful construction lines pale.

reflection: Does the rim ellipse match the angle of the cup you observed?
Can you identify the body volume and handle loop in your drawing?
Which construction line or edge did you change after looking back?
extension: Turn the cup to a new angle and make a quick second construction, checking how the rim ellipse and handle opening change.

teaching.whyItMatters: A simple volume gives you a way to place the cup in space, while observation keeps the drawing from turning into a generic cylinder.
teaching.connections: Return to Lesson 4's comparative measurement: check the cup's total height against its width before detailing. The axis and ellipse guide add depth to those proportion checks, and this construction prepares you to compare bowl rims by eye height in Lesson 9.

deepDive: A cylinder is a useful way to think about a cup's body: a center axis helps keep the sides organized, and elliptical openings suggest the circular rim and base in perspective. Treat that structure as a guide rather than a template. A cup can narrow toward its base, lean slightly, or have a rim that is not perfectly level. Picard's progression from flat shapes to volumes informs this starting construction; the visible silhouette and rim in front of you decide where it needs to change.

The handle belongs to the same object but has its own looped shape and thickness. Find where it meets the body at the top and bottom, then compare the gap inside the handle with the cup's width. A loop attached in the wrong place can make an otherwise plausible body feel unstable. Dodson's draw-through construction is useful for seeing simple forms as volumes, while the ellipse pages support checking the opening. Keep guides light so a measured correction remains easy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keeping a perfect cylinder and guessed handle even when the cup looks different.
commonMistakes.lookFor: The body sides ignore a visible taper, or the handle's opening and attachment points do not match the observed view.
